clusters.name: Early tension with stepfather and chess pressure, 1987
clusters.reason: Around when you began secondary school, distance grew between you and your stepfather while you stayed warm toward your dad. Your stepmother left over disagreement about having a baby, and you made the city chess squad but felt out of your depth, your anxiety rising. These shifts piled up as your family was deciding whether to expand.

clusters.name: Grandfather's death and the year away from conservatory, 1989–1994
clusters.reason: Your grandfather died in mid-1991 while you were in your first term at the conservatory. Around that time your father's father came back into the family after years away. You hurt your wrist and stopped playing within weeks of starting; you and your close friend Rafe had a blow-up and he moved out. You were lost and low, unable to get going, high most days, absorbed in fixing radios. A bleak year followed at community college before an exchange to Portugal turned things around and you tore through your degree. Your symptoms and anxiety stayed high and your functioning stayed down through this stretch, with the injury and your grandfather's death hitting close together.

clusters.name: Performance peak and relationship ending, 1998–1999
clusters.reason: You were playing the best you ever had and winning competitions, but insomnia began getting in the way before concerts though you practised hard. The relationship with Joelle lasted roughly eighteen months and ended in the summer of 1999. You started with a therapist after the split. Your functioning rose even as your symptoms did—a high point as a performer shadowed by sleeplessness and the ending of the relationship.

clusters.name: Burnout, grandmother's illness, and the long slump, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around 2001 you began running out of steam for performing, less content by the month, and your grandmother was found to have bowel cancer. A disastrous audition for the national orchestra followed in 2002; you were done with performing and on poor terms with family and friends. You left Thornbury for Gull Harbour, then met Marisol and moved to Fenwick to live with her within months. When that split came apart in late 2003 you sank into a deep depression. You could not face your family but relied on friends. Your grandmother died in February 2004, the same month you returned to your therapist and began swimming to help you sleep. Your anxiety and symptoms climbed while your functioning fell through this whole stretch, and you were distance from your parents even as you drew toward friends and your therapist.

clusters.name: Grandmother and grandfather's deaths, nursing school, and cutoff from mother, 2008–2009
clusters.reason: Your grandmother died in early 2008 and your grandfather around that time. You took four weeks building at Alder Creek before nursing school; you were too drained for conversation with your mother, she pressed to visit you against your wishes, and the visit went wrong. You stopped speaking to your mother when you moved to Marlow Sound for nursing school that summer; the silence held for roughly a year. Your aunt had a stroke around the same time with months of rehabilitation ahead. The deaths of both grandparents, the conflict with your mother at the lodge, and the cutoff as you left for school all fell within these months.

clusters.name: Marriage, family visits, and sleep struggles with partner's family, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: You married Wren in spring 2017 and saw your mother a bit less once she came along. Within months your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis and your aunt Imogen's memory problems worsened; she lashed out when muddled. Your sister Tara married and had a baby on the way by late 2019. Around late October 2019, Wren became swamped with a street party, fundraising dinner, and drive to the lake for her mother's retirement. You overfunctioned laying out a plan to settle her; she talks with her father and brother all day and nothing happens to one that the others don't hear. You were awake from small hours at the lake weekend with no more sleep and could only pull back as the others rose—you feel you don't belong with her family. Your anxiety and symptoms rose, your functioning fell, and you drew toward overfunctioning with Wren while distancing from her family.
